summary: Founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty, Vijayanagara absorbed the last Hoysala lands by 1346 and the Madurai Sultanate by 1378, uniting the Hindu kingdoms of the south. For two centuries it fought the Bahmani sultans and their successors for the Raichur Doab, and under Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) it covered almost all of India south of the Krishna river. In 1565 the allied Deccan sultanates crushed its army at Talikota and sacked the capital; the Aravidu kings ruled on from Penukonda and later Chandragiri and Vellore until 1646.
details: Vijayanagara was born in the chaos left by Delhi's invasions of the south. In 1336 the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family, commanders who had served the Hoysala king, founded a new state on the Tungabhadra river; later tradition credits the sage Vidyaranya of Sringeri with inspiring them. After the Hoysala king Veera Ballala III was killed fighting the Sultan of Madurai in 1343, his kingdom crumbled, and by 1346 its lands had merged into the Vijayanagara realm. That year Harihara I and the Hoysala queen made grants to the Sringeri monastery on the same day.

To the north lay the Bahmani Sultanate, founded in 1347 by rebel Delhi officers in the Deccan. The two states fought over the fertile Tungabhadra-Krishna doab, the Godavari basin and the Marathwada country. The wars with Sultan Mohammed Shah I were savage: the historian Firishta wrote that the population of the Carnatic took generations to recover. At the Battle of Adoni in 1368 the Bahmanis used a train of artillery, often called the first recorded use of firearms in South Asia, though historians debate this. The doab between the rivers would be fought over for two centuries.

In 1335 the Delhi governor of Madurai had founded an independent Madurai Sultanate, which killed the Hoysala king in 1343. Bukka Raya I's son Kumara Kampana led Vijayanagara's armies south, first destroying the Sambuvaraya dynasty and then invading the sultanate; the historian Bowman dates the conquest to about 1370, and the Srirangam temple was restored in 1371. The last sultan, Ala-ud-Din Sikandar Shah, was killed at Madurai in 1378, and Vijayanagara took formal possession under Harihara II. Kampana's wife Gangadevi celebrated the war in a Sanskrit poem, the Madhura Vijayam. Vijayanagara now reached the southern tip of India.

The wars over the doab went on under Harihara II (1377-1404), who consolidated the empire beyond the Krishna, and under his son Deva Raya I. The Bahmani sultan Firuz Shah defeated Vijayanagara in 1398 and again in 1406. The peace that followed, dated 1407 in the Vijayanagara article, required Deva Raya to pay an annual tribute of 100,000 huns, five maunds of pearls and fifty elephants, and to give his daughter to the sultan in marriage. When Vijayanagara stopped paying, the Bahmanis invaded again in 1417. Such tribute wars recurred throughout the 15th century.

The tide turned in 1420. Firuz Shah attacked the fort of Pangal, but the campaign went badly for him: his army was beaten, and he retreated and gave up the southern and eastern districts of his kingdom. The defeat broke him, and in 1422 he was forced to abdicate in favour of his brother Ahmad Shah. For Vijayanagara, Pangal undid the humiliation of 1406 and strengthened its hold on the eastern doab. Deva Raya I died in 1422; after the brief reigns of Ramachandra Raya and Vira Vijaya Bukka Raya, Deva Raya II came to the throne.

Deva Raya II, king from 1424, is considered by many the greatest ruler of the Sangama dynasty. He quelled rebellious lords and the Zamorin of Calicut and the ruler of Quilon in Kerala, and his commander Lakkanna collected tribute in Sri Lanka. By 1436 the chiefs of Kondavidu and the Velama rulers had accepted his overlordship, and he fought the Gajapatis of Odisha several times. He wrote in Kannada and Sanskrit and patronised poets such as Kumara Vyasa and Srinatha. The Persian envoy Abdur Razzak, writing around 1443, said the empire stretched from Ceylon to Gulbarga.

After some years of peace, war with the Bahmani Sultanate broke out again in 1443. Firishta blamed Deva Raya II's military build-up, which included recruiting many Muslim archers and cavalry; Abdur Razzak said the sultan exploited a revolt at Vijayanagara, including a brother's attempt to assassinate the king, who was wounded. The fighting brought some successes and some reversals. In the end Vijayanagara forces fell back to Mudgal, and some land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna was lost. The Bahmani sultan later celebrated with the Chand Minar at Daulatabad. It was the last major conflict between the two powers.

Deva Raya II died in 1446 and was succeeded by his son Mallikarjuna Raya. The Gajapati king of Odisha took advantage, occupying the Reddi kingdoms of Rajahmundry and Kondaveedu and reaching Kanchipuram and Tiruchirappalli, ending Vijayanagara control over much of the Tamil country. An inscription mocked the Gajapati as 'a yawning lion to the sheep of the Karnatak King'. Under Mallikarjuna's successor Virupaksha Raya II, Goa and much of Karnataka were lost to the Bahmani Sultanate. The empire was shrinking on several sides at once, and its prestige had fallen far.

Virupaksha Raya II's governor Saluva Narasimha limited the damage. He held almost all of coastal Andhra south of the Krishna, Chittoor, the two Arcots and Kolar, defeated the Gajapatis and took Udayagiri, drove the Pandyas from Tanjore and recovered most of the empire's earlier losses. After Virupaksha Raya II died in 1485, Saluva Narasimha led a coup that ended the Sangama dynasty and founded the Saluva dynasty. He left his young sons in the care of the general Tuluva Narasa Nayaka, who ruled as regent until 1503 and defended the empire against the Gajapatis and the Bahmanis.

In 1503 Narasa Nayaka's son Vira Narasimha had the last Saluva prince killed and began the Tuluva dynasty, but nobles revolted and neighbours encroached. In 1509 his brother Krishnadevaraya came to the throne. That year his forces clashed with the Bahmani sultan Mahmud and Bijapur's Yusuf Adil Shah at Diwani; Mahmud was wounded and defeated, Yusuf was killed, and the Raichur Doab was annexed, according to his biography. Krishnadevaraya then released Mahmud and restored him as ruler. In 1510 he made friends with the Portuguese in Goa, buying guns and Arabian horses from them.

Krishnadevaraya then turned east against the resurgent Gajapati kingdom of Odisha under King Prataparudra, which held the coastal Andhra forts. The siege of Udayagiri began in 1512 and lasted about a year. Next Kondaveedu fell to a night attack led by his minister Timmarusu. Prataparudra eventually came to terms, giving his daughter Jaganmohini to Krishnadevaraya in marriage, and the Krishna river became the boundary between the two kingdoms. A defeat at Pangal by Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda in 1513 showed the limits of his power, but the east coast south of the Krishna was now Vijayanagara's.

Raichur, the great fortress of the doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra, had changed hands many times. In 1520 Krishnadevaraya besieged it, held by Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur, with an army said to number hundreds of thousands of foot soldiers. On 19 May 1520, after a hard siege in which some 16,000 Vijayanagara soldiers are said to have died, the fortress fell, with help from Portuguese gunners under Cristovao de Figueiredo. Krishnadevaraya went on to occupy Bijapur and later razed Gulbarga. The empire was at its peak, and Babur considered him the most powerful ruler in India.

Krishnadevaraya was followed by his half-brother Achyuta Deva Raya (1529-1542). When Achyuta died in June 1542, his brother-in-law Salakaraju Tirumala took power as regent for the boy king Venkata I, had him killed and even invited the Sultan of Bijapur to help him. Outraged nobles rallied to Rama Raya, Krishnadevaraya's son-in-law, who backed Achyuta's nephew Sadasiva Raya. In 1543 Salakaraju was defeated and killed at the Battle of the Tungabhadra. Sadasiva became emperor, but Rama Raya held real power for the next two decades, meddling in the quarrels of the Deccan sultanates.

Rama Raya's policy of playing the sultanates off against one another finally united them against him. Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda and Bidar joined forces, and on 23 January 1565 they met his army near Talikota, by the Krishna river. The battle seemed to be going Vijayanagara's way until, according to some accounts, two Muslim generals in its service, the Gilani brothers, changed sides. Rama Raya was captured and beheaded, and his army fled in confusion. The sultanate armies plundered the capital unopposed; its royal centre was never rebuilt, and the empire's centre of gravity moved south.

Tirumala Deva Raya, one of the Vijayanagara commanders at Talikota, escaped with the army. He tried to regroup at Vijayanagara and used the ruined city for about two years, then founded a new capital at Penukonda and began the Aravidu dynasty. In 1572 he abdicated, dividing what remained among his three sons. The Aravidu kings later moved their capital to Chandragiri (1592) and Vellore (1604), but central authority collapsed in 1614 and the empire ended in 1646. Nayaka rulers at Madurai, Tanjore, Gingee, Mysore and Keladi became independent kingdoms.
